name: Corkscrew Route

approach_logistics.trailhead: Sloan Peak climbers' pullout (FR-49, Sloan Creek Road)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the unsigned Sloan Peak climbers' pullout on FR-49 (Sloan Creek Road, ~1,900 ft), crossing the North Fork Sauk River

approach: The standard approach starts from the unsigned Sloan Peak climbers'-trail pullout on FR 49 (Sloan Creek Road, reached via SR 530 south of Darrington) at roughly 1,900 ft, on the north side of the North Fork Sauk River — not the maintained North Fork Sauk River Trail #649, but a boot path a short distance further along FR 49. From the pullout the path is flat and brushy (stinging nettle, then devil's club) for a few tenths of a mile before dropping to the North Fork Sauk River, which must be forded or crossed on logs (log jams are usually adequate about 0.5 mi in; they shift year to year and can be dicey in high water/early season). The path fords the river braids two to three times over the next mile, then follows Cougar Creek upstream on a faint, cairned/flagged track through sandy streambed and forest — expect route-finding to be slow here, especially with snow on the ground into early summer. Around 3,000–3,200 ft the trail crosses Cougar Creek itself (can be impassable lower down; look for a crossing around 3.2K ft) and climbs steeply through switchbacks in forest, passing a waterfall on Cougar Creek near 5,000 ft (roughly 2–2.5 hrs from the car, and the last reliable water before the basin). Above the falls the climbers' path breaks out of the trees onto scree and slabs, angling up to the 5,800 ft saddle/basin on Sloan's northeast side (reached ~4–5 hrs in for most parties), with a small stream and possible campsite in the basin — the standard overnight/base camp spot for a two-day ascent. From the basin, ledges and slabs lead up to the toe of the Sloan Glacier; rope up and gear up (crampons, axe, glacier kit) here before crossing onto the ice toward the southeast edge of the summit massif. An alternate, often-preferred approach uses the Bedal Creek trailhead (FS 4096, a rough 3-mile 4WD spur off the Mountain Loop Highway, ~2,790 ft) and the old Bedal Creek trail/climbers' path to the same 5,300 ft Bedal–Sloan saddle, avoiding the North Fork Sauk fords entirely at the cost of a rougher access road; total stats by that line run about 9.5 mi and 5,300 ft round trip. Either way, expect avalanche/snow-slope hazard on the basin and glacier approach into early summer, one notable open crevasse on the Sloan Glacier that's typically snow-bridged in normal season, and generally loose, brushy, unmaintained tread below treeline on both approaches.

waypoints.name: Bedal Creek / Bedal Basin Trailhead (end of FR 4096)
waypoints.directions: Drive the Mountain Loop Highway to Forest Road 4096 and follow that rough, narrow spur - a 4WD road about three miles long where high clearance genuinely helps - to its end at the Bedal Creek trailhead, around 2,790 feet.

waypoints.name: Climber's trail turnoff on Bedal Creek Trail
waypoints.directions: Walk the old Bedal Creek Trail about 1.5 miles and 700 ft to around 3,500 ft, where a climbers' path, often marked with pink flagging, turns off to the left. Watch for it: the old tread continues and dies in a brushy washout below the basin.

waypoints.name: Sloan Peak Summit
waypoints.directions: Climb the path steeply through forest to talus near 4,900 ft, then bend southeast to the Bedal-Sloan saddle at 5,300 ft. Continue southeast over a rock ridge near 5,800 ft, rope up and cross the Sloan Glacier southwest to the rock near 7,100 ft. Follow the exposed heather shelf of the Corkscrew across the south face onto the west face, climb the gully to the crest, then a short class 4 step and third class to the summit.

descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent line: from the summit, downclimb the short, low-5th-class/exposed Class 4 step about 100 ft below the true summit (the 'bear hug' move on the ridge has solid hand cracks on both sides and is usually downclimbed free by competent parties). Parties uncomfortable downclimbing it can rig a short hand line or single-strand rappel here — there is no fixed/bolted anchor; build off a rock horn, chockstone, or gear placement, and a single 30 m/60 m rope doubled is more than enough for the ~15-20 ft of steep rock involved. Below that, follow cairns and the climbers' trail back along the south-face heather ledges and the loose scree/dirt gully that gained access from the ledge system — this gully is notably loose underfoot and the ledges above it have real exposure (parties have noted a ~500 ft unprotected drop at the outer edge), so downclimb it carefully rather than glissading or rushing. At the base of the gully/ledges, re-rope for the glacier crossing back to the toe where gear was staged, then continue down slabs to the 5,800 ft basin/saddle. From there it's a full reversal of whichever approach was used — steep scree/slab and forest switchbacks back to the Cougar Creek waterfall and North Fork Sauk crossings (Sloan Creek/FR 49 approach), or the Bedal Creek climbers' path and old trail (Bedal Creek/FS 4096 approach) — down to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb descent with no standard rappelling on the glacier or ledges; the only rope use besides glacier travel is the optional short hand line/rappel off the summit step described above. Total car-to-car time for strong parties runs roughly 9-13 hours depending on approach and conditions; snow lingering on the basin/ledges into early summer, and afternoon softening of the glacier snowpack on hot days, are the main descent-timing hazards.
